LAUNCHFORGE PARTNER BUSINESS CASE — HUMAN-CURATED VERSION

Executive decision: validate a productionisation platform for founders who already have an agent-generated mobile prototype but lack the engineering, security, compliance and operational capability to launch it safely. The product accepts a repository or project archive, diagnoses dependencies and risk, proposes a remediation plan, provisions backend, database, storage, secrets, observability and CI/CD, creates a landing page and admin console, connects Stripe and Google authentication, prepares store assets and submission checklists, then supports governed AI-assisted rebuilds and hosting.

Product boundary: LaunchForge may automate preparation and deployment steps, but must never promise automatic App Store or Google Play approval. Developer-account ownership, legal declarations, privacy content, regulated-category review and final release authorization remain human-controlled external gates.

Target customer: non-technical or lightly technical founders, venture studios and agencies with working prototypes whose next bottleneck is production readiness rather than ideation. The job to be done is not code generation; it is turning uncertain generated code into an operated product with explicit ownership, evidence and rollback.

Customer journey: upload and consent; code, dependency, license and secret scan; risk classification; priced remediation scope; infrastructure blueprint; controlled build; authentication and payment setup; admin and landing surfaces; observability and incident controls; store-readiness pack; human approval; release; continued development through versioned rebuilds.

Commercial hypothesis: USD 20 monthly platform fee plus usage tokens for rebuilds. A launch offer may additionally charge 5% of app revenue plus rebuild tokens. This is not an approved price. Revenue share introduces reconciliation, tax, attribution and founder-alignment risks and should be tested against a simpler subscription-plus-usage alternative.

Differentiation hypothesis: production evidence, governed rebuilds, multi-service orchestration and release operations in one founder-facing workflow. The moat cannot be a wrapper around coding agents. It must come from reusable deployment blueprints, risk policies, integration reliability, store-readiness knowledge, incident history and partner distribution.

Scope and methodology: this case uses only the founder brief. Demand, conversion, costs, margins, support load and timing are hypotheses. Evidence must come from founder interviews, prototype audits, vendor quotes, security testing and paid pilots. No market statistic, traction claim, testimonial or financial history is asserted.

Scenarios: downside means heterogeneous projects create high manual support, rebuild tokens have weak margin and store failures damage trust; narrow accepted frameworks or stop. Base means selected stacks pass a standardized pathway with bounded remediation and recurring hosting; productise those stacks. Upside means venture studios and coding-agent ecosystems provide repeatable portfolios; scale only after isolation, support and release controls are proven.

Partner packages: cloud/infrastructure partner supplies credits and reference architecture; payments partner supports platform and connected-account design; coding-agent partner exports a compatible project manifest; compliance partner reviews privacy and store policy; venture studio supplies a controlled portfolio and buyer feedback.

Decision ask: approve a 90-day validation program, not a public one-click-launch claim. FIZZUP PARTNER BUSINESS CASE — HUMAN-CURATED VERSION

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
FizzUp is a private AI Speaking Coach for adults who already know English but do not reliably access it under real professional pressure. The product is built around one promise: help a person prepare for, conduct and learn from the conversations that matter. The current system is a real full stack — Flutter mobile client, Node/Fastify/Postgres backend, authentication, personal memory, billing integration and AI voice and text providers. iOS 1.0.0 build 45 passed Apple review. Commercial pricing, paid conversion and learning outcomes beyond current product evidence remain hypotheses.

The proposed partnership is a controlled 90-day enterprise pilot for Polish B1–C1 professionals. FizzUp provides private coaching; the employer receives activation and privacy-safe aggregate outcomes, never individual mistakes, transcripts or private plans. The decision requested by 30 September 2026 is to nominate one sponsor, select a cohort, approve privacy boundaries and agree success and stop criteria.

THE CUSTOMER PROBLEM
Professionals often understand English but underperform in high-stakes meetings, negotiations and presentations. Traditional courses separate practice from the moment of need. Generic AI chat does not preserve a governed learning loop or prove that useful language becomes available later. Employers want improved communication but cannot ethically obtain it through surveillance.

PRODUCT AND USER JOURNEY
1. Prepare — the learner names an upcoming real moment, audience and desired outcome.
2. Speak — a private AI Native conducts a realtime voice exchange calibrated to the situation.
3. Review — the learner sees useful phrases actually used and moments that constrained clarity.
4. Upgrade — FizzUp proposes natural ways to express the same intended meaning more effectively.
5. Practise — the learner actively produces the improved language across varied contexts.
6. Transfer — later sessions test whether the language returns under pressure.
7. Progress — evidence describes observable speaking behavior, not vanity scores.

The product center is voice. Every supporting surface must improve the next conversation, preserve its value or make credible progress visible.

WHAT IS SHIPPED, WHAT IS DIRECTION
Verified today: functioning mobile and backend architecture, authentication, memory mechanisms, billing integration, voice and text provider integrations, and an Apple-reviewed iOS release baseline. Strategic direction: paid tiers, enterprise entitlement, scaled company content and broader automotive or omnichannel continuity. Unproven: willingness to pay, employer conversion, sustained learning transfer and voice-cost economics. These boundaries must remain explicit in every partner claim.

VALUE FOR PARTNERS
Enterprise pilot partners obtain a structured communication-development program without access to private learner content. Distribution partners gain a differentiated adult-learning proposition tied to real work. Content partners can supply governed scenarios and materials without turning FizzUp into a course catalogue. Technology partners can improve voice reliability, latency and cost while respecting tenant and privacy boundaries.

DIFFERENTIATION AND DEFENSIBILITY
FizzUp does not compete on the number of lessons or AI utilities. Its defensibility hypothesis combines a personal relationship with an AI Native, four-layer memory, real-moment context, deliberate language reuse and evidence of transfer. The durable asset is not a transcript archive; it is a privacy-governed model of what helps a particular learner communicate better. Defensibility must be proven through return behavior, successful delayed reuse and partner trust.

COMMERCIAL MODEL — HYPOTHESES
B2C may combine a free activation experience with paid voice capacity, deeper preparation and continuity. B2B may use per-participant program pricing or a cohort pilot fee with clear voice allowances. No price is approved in this report. Every package must be tested against conversion, voice cost, support load, gross margin and retention. The company should avoid unlimited voice promises before provider economics are measured.

GO-TO-MARKET
The initial wedge is adult Polish professionals at B1–C1 with identifiable English moments: customer calls, management meetings, interviews and presentations. Acquire users through professional communities, employer pilots and partners already serving internationalising Polish firms. The first commercial motion should sell a measured pilot outcome, not a broad learning platform. Expansion follows evidence: individual paid conversion, team renewal, new markets and channel partnerships.

SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY
This case uses accepted FizzUp product documentation and the founder brief. It does not rely on invented market statistics, testimonials, interviews or financial history. Product facts are separated from management hypotheses. Decisions are staged through observable evidence: first voice success, completed speaking cycles, delayed phrase reuse, return after a real trigger, privacy-safe pilot activation and willingness to pay.

ASSUMPTIONS AND SCENARIOS
Downside: learners try voice once, do not return, and provider cost remains high. Response: reduce scope, improve first success and stop paid acquisition.
Base: a meaningful segment completes repeated cycles, selected employers sponsor pilots and voice economics support a bounded paid allowance. Response: productise one repeatable cohort offer.
Upside: demonstrated transfer and partner-led distribution create renewals across multiple employers. Response: scale only after privacy and support controls remain effective.
No scenario is a forecast until the financial model is approved and linked to measured cohorts.

90-DAY PILOT
Days 1–30: recruit a narrow cohort, verify first voice success, latency and correct workspace isolation.
Days 31–60: measure completed Prepare–Speak–Review–Practise cycles, return frequency and qualitative usefulness without employer access to private details.
Days 61–90: test willingness to pay, aggregate sponsor reporting, voice cost per active participant and a renewal decision.
Success criteria must be agreed before recruitment. Illustrative gates are activation, repeat speaking, evidence of reuse, sponsor trust and sustainable cost. Final numeric thresholds belong to the signed pilot charter.

RISKS, OWNERS AND CONTROLS
Critical — privacy or tenant leakage. Owner: Privacy Lead. Control: explicit workspace boundary, least privilege, aggregate reporting and incident rehearsal.
High — unreliable realtime voice. Owner: CTO. Control: monitored latency, graceful fallback and provider redundancy plan.
High — weak return behavior. Owner: Product Lead. Control: real-moment onboarding, trigger-based preparation and cohort analysis.
High — unsustainable voice economics. Owner: CFO. Control: allowance design, cost telemetry and scenario limits.
Medium — enterprise complexity before product evidence. Owner: Founder. Control: one narrow pilot contract and fixed customization boundary.

12-MONTH ROADMAP
Quarter 1: first-success reliability, instrumentation and pilot charter.
Quarter 2: controlled employer pilot and pricing tests.
Quarter 3: repeatable onboarding, privacy evidence pack and channel enablement.
Quarter 4: scale decision based on retention, transfer evidence, gross margin and sponsor renewal — or narrow the proposition if evidence is insufficient.

PARTNERSHIP PACKAGES
Pilot sponsor: cohort access, accountable executive and success criteria.
Distribution partner: qualified introductions and joint pilot funnel.
Content partner: governed scenarios linked to real professional moments.
Technology partner: voice, observability or security capability with measurable service levels.
Research partner: independent evaluation of speaking transfer without exposing private learner content.

DECISION AND ASK
Approve one 90-day pilot, not a broad rollout. Nominate an accountable sponsor, agree privacy and evidence boundaries, and set a decision meeting for 30 September 2026. Continue only if users return to meaningful voice, useful language transfers into later speech, partners trust the reporting model and unit economics support a paid service. Defensibility must be proven through return behavior, successful delayed reuse and partner trust.

COMMERCIAL MODEL — HYPOTHESES
B2C may combine a free activation experience with paid voice capacity, deeper preparation and continuity. B2B may use per-participant program pricing or a cohort pilot fee with clear voice allowances. No price is approved in this report. Every package must be tested against conversion, voice cost, support load, gross margin and retention. The company should avoid unlimited voice promises before provider economics are measured.

GO-TO-MARKET
The initial wedge is adult Polish professionals at B1–C1 with identifiable English moments: customer calls, management meetings, interviews and presentations. Acquire users through professional communities, employer pilots and partners already serving internationalising Polish firms. The first commercial motion should sell a measured pilot outcome, not a broad learning platform. Expansion follows evidence: individual paid conversion, team renewal, new markets and channel partnerships.

SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY
This case uses accepted FizzUp product documentation and the founder brief. It does not rely on invented market statistics, testimonials, interviews or financial history. Product facts are separated from management hypotheses. Decisions are staged through observable evidence: first voice success, completed speaking cycles, delayed phrase reuse, return after a real trigger, privacy-safe pilot activation and willingness to pay.

ASSUMPTIONS AND SCENARIOS
Downside: learners try voice once, do not return, and provider cost remains high. Response: reduce scope, improve first success and stop paid acquisition.
Base: a meaningful segment completes repeated cycles, selected employers sponsor pilots and voice economics support a bounded paid allowance. Response: productise one repeatable cohort offer.
Upside: demonstrated transfer and partner-led distribution create renewals across multiple employers. Response: scale only after privacy and support controls remain effective.
No scenario is a forecast until the financial model is approved and linked to measured cohorts.

90-DAY PILOT
Days 1–30: recruit a narrow cohort, verify first voice success, latency and correct workspace isolation.
Days 31–60: measure completed Prepare–Speak–Review–Practise cycles, return frequency and qualitative usefulness without employer access to private details.
Days 61–90: test willingness to pay, aggregate sponsor reporting, voice cost per active participant and a renewal decision.
Success criteria must be agreed before recruitment. Illustrative gates are activation, repeat speaking, evidence of reuse, sponsor trust and sustainable cost. Final numeric thresholds belong to the signed pilot charter.

RISKS, OWNERS AND CONTROLS
Critical — privacy or tenant leakage. Owner: Privacy Lead. Control: explicit workspace boundary, least privilege, aggregate reporting and incident rehearsal.
High — unreliable realtime voice. Owner: CTO. Control: monitored latency, graceful fallback and provider redundancy plan.
High — weak return behavior. Owner: Product Lead. Control: real-moment onboarding, trigger-based preparation and cohort analysis.
High — unsustainable voice economics. Owner: CFO. Control: allowance design, cost telemetry and scenario limits.
Medium — enterprise complexity before product evidence. Owner: Founder. Control: one narrow pilot contract and fixed customization boundary.

12-MONTH ROADMAP
Quarter 1: first-success reliability, instrumentation and pilot charter.
Quarter 2: controlled employer pilot and pricing tests.
Quarter 3: repeatable onboarding, privacy evidence pack and channel enablement.
Quarter 4: scale decision based on retention, transfer evidence, gross margin and sponsor renewal — or narrow the proposition if evidence is insufficient.

PARTNERSHIP PACKAGES
Pilot sponsor: cohort access, accountable executive and success criteria.
Distribution partner: qualified introductions and joint pilot funnel.
Content partner: governed scenarios linked to real professional moments.
Technology partner: voice, observability or security capability with measurable service levels.
Research partner: independent evaluation of speaking transfer without exposing private learner content.

DECISION AND ASK
Approve one 90-day pilot, not a broad rollout. Nominate an accountable sponsor, agree privacy and evidence boundaries, and set a decision meeting for 30 September 2026. Continue only if users return to meaningful voice, useful language transfers into later speech, partners trust the reporting model and unit economics support a paid service.
